text: Greene’s lumbering supply trains, field guns, and their Continental infantry escort rolled from Guilford Courthouse on 10 February toward the lower fords of the Dan River at Irwin’s and Boyd’s Ferries (at today’s South Boston, Virginia). Williams’s flying army marched westward to gain contact with the British and led them northward toward Dix’s Ferry on the upper Dan—thereby distracting Cornwallis from the movement of the main body. American and loyalist dragoons clashed at Bruce’s Mill, only 7 miles from Guilford Courthouse. The Americans ended the skirmish by tearing planks from a bridge spanning Reedy Fork Creek, forcing Tarleton’s dragoons on a costly detour while Williams’s soldiers force marched toward Dix’s Ferry. From 11 to 13 February, Cornwallis relentlessly drove his army after the American light troops, hindered by hasty obstacles and harassing attacks by local rebel militiamen. Sgt. Maj. William Seymour of the Delaware Regiment later described the withdrawal:On the eighth instant [8 February], we marched from here, General Greene’s army taking one road and the light troops another. . . . This day we received intelligence that the British Army was advancing very close in our rear. . . . We marched . . . on the ninth inst., taking the road towards Dan River, which we reached on the fourteenth, after a march of two hundred and fifty miles from . . . our encampment at Pacolet River . . . we marched for the most part both day and night, the main of the British being close in our rear, so that we had not scarce time to cook our victuals, their whole attention being on our light troops. In the meantime, Greene’s troops and camp followers crossed the Dan River on light boats while engineers used the bateaux to carry across the heavy wagons and cannons. The army finished its movement by midday on 14 February, prompting Greene to send a

message to Williams ordering him to break contact and withdraw to Boyd’s Ferry. Williams’s corps outdistanced the pursuing British and safely crossed by torchlight at Boyd’s Ferry, with Greene, Williams, and Lee in the last boats. Tarleton’s advance guard reached Irwin’s Ferry early on 15 February, only to find “some works evacuated, which had been constructed to cover the retreat of the enemy, who six hours before had finished their passage, and were then encamped on the opposite bank. Every measure of the Americans, during their march from the Catawba to Virginia, was judiciously designed and vigorously executed.”While the American troops rested from their exertions, General Greene implemented measures to retain the initiative. He believed Cornwallis had three possible options: move to the proloyalist Hillsborough region for recruits and supplies; continue the pursuit into Virginia; or establish communications with General Arnold’s army via the Roanoke River at Halifax, North Carolina. Greene sent Steuben to prevent Arnold’s army from leaving Portsmouth, Virginia, and Kosciusko to fortify Halifax. Greene urged Governor Thomas Jefferson of Virginia and Governor Abner Nash of North Carolina to call out their available alarm militia and state line units to reinforce the Continentals. Greene quickly reassessed his campaign plan after learning Cornwallis’s army was regrouping in North Carolina, as he noted to Governor Jefferson:When the Enemy first took their departure from the Dan they had every prospect of great reinforcements from the Tories of Carolina . . . if they were permitted to roam at large in the State that it would indubitably impress the idea of Conquest upon the Minds of the disaffected . . . and perhaps occasion those . . . to take an active and decisive part against us. I instantly determined . . . to advance into the state. . . . It was necessary to convince the Carolinians that they were not conquered and by affording immediate protection . . . engage the continuance of their confidence and friendship.
citation: Skinner, Harold Allen, Jr. The War in the Carolinas and Georgia, 1781–1782. U.S. Army Campaigns of the Revolutionary War, CMH Pub 71-52. Washington, D.C.: Center of Military History, United States Army, 2026.
